summary: The paper investigates how the choice of effective Hamiltonian affects predictive quantum control for transmon qubits, comparing the standard Duffing approximation with a more faithful diagonalized-transmon model that retains the full cosine potential's spectral and control-operator properties. Correction fields derived from the Duffing Hamiltonian substantially reduce error within that model but fail to transfer effectively to an independently calibrated diagonalized-transmon baseline pulse, demonstrating that small differences in transition frequencies and charge-matrix elements compound during driven evolution into substantially different dynamical error generators.
motivation: Accurate effective Hamiltonians are essential for reliable open-loop quantum control, yet agreement on static spectral quantities does not guarantee predictive accuracy under driven evolution. For fast transmon gates where leakage and AC Stark shifts become significant, evaluating whether an approximate Hamiltonian correctly predicts the multilevel correction required by more faithful system descriptions is critical.
method: The authors constructed correction pulses using the Magnus-based constrained-control framework applied separately to a Duffing Hamiltonian and a diagonalized-transmon model with four-level truncation justified by a sequential-transition estimate. They tested transferability via a hybrid protocol combining Duffing-derived corrections with diagonalized-transmon-calibrated baseline pulses, while isolating model dependence through analysis of accumulated AC Stark phase.
result: At $|\alpha_2| t_f = 5.74$ (fast-gate regime), the hybrid protocol achieves average fidelity error at least a factor of $\sim 2\text{–}3$ worse than self-consistent diagonalized-transmon correction; the AC Stark phase mismatch between models reaches $\sim 5\text{–}10\%$ for $E_J/E_C = 30\text{–}50$. A four-level model reveals higher-order error channels missed by three-level truncations, enabling nonlinear corrections that outperform linear strategies by $\sim$ one order of magnitude at longer gate times while using identical physical control resources.
